must_remember: Division of amplitude splits a single incident ray into reflected and refracted parts, ensuring sustained interference from coherent secondary beams.
A light wave reflecting at a denser medium boundary (rarer to denser) suffers an abrupt phase change of $\pi$ radians (path retardation of $\lambda / 2$).
The optical path difference for a parallel-sided thin film in reflected light is given by $\Delta = 2\mu t \cos(r) \pm \frac{\lambda}{2}$.
Constructive interference in reflected light occurs when $2\mu t \cos(r) = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$.
Destructive interference in reflected light occurs when $2\mu t \cos(r) = n\lambda$.
The central spot in Newton's rings formed by reflected light is dark due to a $\pi$ phase change at the point of contact.
The radius of the $n$-th dark ring in Newton's rings is given by $r_n = \sqrt{nR\lambda}$.
Fringe width in an air wedge film is expressed as $\beta = \frac{\lambda}{2\mu \theta}$.

glossary.meaning: A phenomenon where the amplitude of an incident wavefront is divided into two or more parts by partial reflection and refraction at an interface.
Principle describing the phase relationship between reflected and refracted light waves at a boundary.
The geometrical path length multiplied by the refractive index of the medium ($\mu t$).
Interference fringes of equal thickness formed by wedge-shaped or variable-thickness films like air films in Newton's rings.
The angle formed between two reflecting surfaces meeting at an edge, determining the fringe width in a wedge film.
